items.q: An industrial motion controller needs latency under 10 ms while a smart-agriculture soil sensor tolerates a 2–5 s delay. This contrast best illustrates which criterion driving connectivity choice?
items.explain: Latency requirements differ by orders of magnitude across use cases; real-time control demands very low latency, while non-critical telemetry can tolerate seconds — a primary selection criterion.

items.q: A router differs from a switch in an Ethernet IoT network primarily because the router:
options: Forwards frames using MAC addresses at Layer 2
Operates at Layer 3, performs NAT, and acts as the gateway between the LAN and the WAN/internet
items.explain: The switch is a Layer-2 device forwarding by MAC within the LAN. The router is a Layer-3 device performing NAT (private↔public IP) and routing to the WAN — the gateway to the internet.

items.q: Which TSN mechanism allows an urgent sensor frame to interrupt a lower-priority frame already being transmitted?
items.explain: Frame Preemption (802.1Qbu/802.3br) lets urgent/time-critical frames preempt lower-priority ones in transit, so life-critical data is never stuck behind bulk traffic.

items.q: The fundamental trade-off accepted by using the unlicensed 2.4 GHz ISM band is:
options: Interference — it is a crowded 'commons' shared by Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, microwaves, etc.
Inability to scale to many devices
items.explain: Unlicensed bands are free and global, but everyone uses them, so the price is congestion/interference — which is why robust techniques (DSSS, channel agility) and sub-GHz options exist.

items.q: Zigbee's network layer routing is described as 'AODV-like (on-demand)'. What does this mean?
options: All routes are pre-computed and fixed
When a path is unknown, the source floods a Route Request (RREQ) and the destination replies with a Route Reply (RREP); routes are discovered as needed
Routing is done only by the cloud
items.explain: On-demand (AODV-like) routing discovers paths only when needed: an RREQ flood finds the destination, which returns an RREP. Route maintenance repairs broken links using neighbour tables/LQI.

items.q: Which layer of the Zigbee stack is provided by IEEE 802.15.4 (rather than Zigbee itself)?
items.explain: 802.15.4 provides the PHY and MAC (radios, channels, CSMA/CA, ACKs). Zigbee adds NWK (routing), APS (security/binding), and the application/ZCL cluster model on top.

items.q: In BLE GATT, the difference between a Notification and an Indication is:
options: Notifications are encrypted; Indications are not
Notifications have no GATT-level acknowledgment; Indications require an acknowledgment (for critical data)
items.explain: Notifications push data without a GATT-level ACK (efficient telemetry). Indications require an ACK, used for critical changes needing confirmation — a reliability-vs-overhead trade-off.

items.q: Why is BLE often called the cheapest IoT gateway option?
options: Virtually every smartphone already supports BLE, so the user's phone acts as the gateway
items.explain: Because nearly all smartphones/tablets speak BLE, the gateway is already in the user's pocket — no extra hub needed (unlike Zigbee, which needs a dedicated coordinator/hub).

items.q: Why is a battery-powered coin-cell sensor rarely built on standard Wi-Fi?
options: Standard Wi-Fi is power-hungry, draining small batteries quickly — it suits mains-powered devices
items.explain: Standard Wi-Fi's high power consumption makes it ill-suited to coin-cell devices; it shines for plugged-in, high-throughput devices. Wi-Fi HaLow (sub-GHz) addresses low-power IoT.

items.q: A LoRaWAN gateway is described as 'transparent'. This means it:
options: Decrypts and interprets the application data
Simply relays LoRa RF packets to the network server as IP without interpreting them; multiple gateways may receive the same message
items.explain: Gateways are transparent relays: they convert LoRa RF to IP and forward to the network server without interpreting payloads. Several gateways hearing the same packet provides redundancy (the NS de-duplicates).

items.q: A mains-powered LoRaWAN actuator must be controllable at ANY moment with minimal downlink latency. Which class fits, and why?
options: Class C — a permanently open receive window allows downlink at any time (acceptable since it's mains-powered)
items.explain: Class C keeps the receiver always open for instant downlink, at the cost of power — fine for mains-powered devices. Class A (battery-optimal) only listens briefly after an uplink.

items.q: For a nationwide fleet of moving vehicle trackers needing carrier coverage with no self-deployed gateways, the best fit is:
items.explain: LTE-M provides mobility (handover) and nationwide carrier coverage with no infrastructure to deploy — ideal for moving asset/vehicle tracking. NB-IoT suits stationary low-rate sensors.

items.q: Which transport-layer mapping is correct for IoT application protocols?
options: MQTT over UDP; CoAP over TCP
MQTT and HTTP over TCP; CoAP and DDS over UDP
CoAP over TCP; HTTP over UDP
items.explain: MQTT, HTTP, and AMQP run over TCP (reliable). CoAP and DDS run over UDP (lightweight, lower overhead for constrained/lossy links).

items.q: Choosing MQTT QoS 0 vs QoS 2 for routine temperature telemetry vs a financial transaction reflects which trade-off?
options: Reliability vs overhead/battery — higher QoS costs round-trips, so use the lowest level the data can tolerate
items.explain: Higher QoS guarantees delivery but adds handshakes (overhead, battery). Routine telemetry can use QoS 0 (fire-and-forget); critical financial/control data warrants QoS 2 (exactly once).

items.q: An MQTT 'retained message' is useful because it:
options: Stores the last value on a topic so a NEW subscriber immediately receives the current state instead of waiting for the next publish
items.explain: A retained message lets the broker hand a newly-connected subscriber the last known value on a topic right away — useful for state (e.g., 'door is closed') rather than waiting for the next update.

items.q: How does a CoAP client achieve reliable delivery over unreliable UDP?
options: It uses Confirmable (CON) messages that expect an ACK; if none arrives, the message is retransmitted
It floods the network with copies
items.explain: CoAP adds optional reliability on top of UDP via Confirmable (CON) messages with ACKs and retransmission. Non-confirmable (NON) messages are fire-and-forget. Message IDs detect duplicates.

items.q: A unique capability CoAP has that neither HTTP nor MQTT offers is:
options: Multicast support (one request reaching many devices), plus the Observe option for resource subscriptions
items.explain: Built on UDP, CoAP supports multicast (one-to-many requests) and the Observe option (subscribe to a resource's changes) — capabilities HTTP and MQTT lack in this comparison.

items.q: In a SCADA system, the component that collects field data and executes local control logic at a remote site is the:
options: RTU / PLC (Remote Terminal Unit / Programmable Logic Controller)
items.explain: RTUs/PLCs sit at the field, gathering sensor data and running local control, then communicate with the SCADA master/HMI (operator interface) over a network (Modbus/DNP3/IP).
